screens.title: Hybrid Cloud Networking & AWS Site-to-Site VPN
screens.narratorSegment: Hybrid cloud networking is the practice of linking an organization’s private data center with public cloud services so data and applications can move between both environments securely and reliably. You will learn why enterprises choose hybrid models — for compliance, data residency, staggered migration, disaster recovery, and predictable burst capacity — and how networking is the backbone that makes those benefits real. This chapter focuses on AWS Site-to-Site VPN: a practical, internet-based, encrypted connection that can be deployed quickly and used as a primary or backup link. We will look at the core components you must provision in AWS and on-premises, explain the role of IPsec, IKE, and ESP in establishing secure tunnels, and point out the common configuration mistakes that cause tunnel failures. By the end you will be able to decide when Site-to-Site VPN is the right choice, identify VGW and CGW roles, and enumerate a concise checklist for a reliable deployment. Think about a real system you manage: what on-premises service would you move behind a VPN first, and why?

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Introduction
Hybrid Cloud Networking & AWS Site-to-Site VPN
Secure, resilient encrypted tunnels to extend your on-premises network into AWS.
In this lesson

You will learn the components of an AWS VPN, why IPsec and IKE matter, and how to choose between VPN and Direct Connect based on bandwidth, latency, and cost.

Coming up

Explore Key Topics
Hybrid drivers
Compliance, migration, disaster recovery, and burst capacity shape hybrid choices.
VPN fundamentals
IPsec, IKE, ESP, and the dual-tunnel redundancy model provide secure connectivity.
Design checklist
Public IP, NAT, ports and routing must be validated before establishing tunnels.
Concept map
On-premises network (CGW)
IPsec tunnels (ESP + IKE)
AWS VPC (VGW)
Why this matters
A well-designed hybrid network preserves security and performance while enabling cloud benefits. Small configuration errors can block traffic even when tunnels show as up, so preparation and testing are essential.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives map to the practical skills you need to design and operate hybrid connectivity with AWS. First, you will explain hybrid cloud networking: what it is, why enterprises use it, and the scenarios where hybrid models win. Second, you will identify all the components of an AWS Site-to-Site VPN — Virtual Private Gateway, Customer Gateway, and the dual IPsec tunnels — and describe each component’s role in establishing secure connectivity. Third, you will differentiate between hybrid connectivity options such as Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect, deciding where each is appropriate based on bandwidth, latency, and cost. Fourth, you will describe how IPsec and IKE secure communications and recognize common design patterns and pitfalls when integrating on-premises networks with AWS. Each objective links a conceptual understanding to practical activities you will perform: planning, provisioning, and troubleshooting a VPN-based connection. Keep these objectives in mind as questions you can answer with a checklist or configuration plan.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills and Checks
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond conceptual knowledge, these objectives emphasize practical checks you will perform during a hybrid deployment. You will learn to verify the public IP and NAT posture of your on-premises gateway so AWS can reach its peer. You will learn to match IPsec parameters and pre-shared keys precisely to avoid tunnel negotiation failures. You will learn to check route propagation and ensure that VPC route tables and on-premises routers both know how to reach each other’s CIDRs. Finally, you will acquire the ability to choose a connectivity option: for moderate bandwidth and quick setup, Site-to-Site VPN often fits; for dedicated, low-latency needs, Direct Connect may be preferred. Each of these objectives links to a hands-on validation step you can test in your environment. After this chapter, you should be able to produce a short deployment checklist and a troubleshooting flow for tunnel and routing problems.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Objectives — Skills
Validation checklist
  • Confirm public-facing IP for the on-premises VPN device; it must match the Customer Gateway entry in AWS.
  • Ensure UDP ports 500 and 4500 are allowed through firewalls and NAT devices for IKE and IPsec NAT traversal.
  • Verify matching IPsec parameters and the pre-shared key on both sides before attempting negotiation.
  • Propagate or add routes so AWS VPC route tables and on-premises routers know each other’s CIDRs.
Practical hints
Use Site-to-Site VPN for moderate bandwidth and quick deployments. Use Direct Connect where dedicated capacity and consistent latency are required. Consider VPN as a backup to Direct Connect to preserve availability.

screens.title: What is Hybrid Cloud Networking?
screens.narratorSegment: Hybrid cloud networking connects an organization’s on-premises systems with public cloud infrastructure so applications and data can operate across both environments securely. The defining trait is seamless, managed connectivity that preserves trust boundaries for sensitive workloads while enabling elasticity for others. Major drivers include compliance and data residency rules that require certain datasets to remain on-premises, phased migration strategies where legacy systems stay local while new services run in the cloud, disaster recovery plans that use the cloud as a secondary site, and burst capacity needs for seasonal peaks. For example, a company may keep its ERP on-premises for regulatory reasons but use AWS for analytics and development: analytics jobs access operational data across a VPN and run on scalable cloud instances. A common misconception is assuming hybrid equals slow; properly designed links, route planning, and placement of latency-sensitive services avoid performance bottlenecks. To design responsibly, inventory which applications need low latency, which require encryption in transit, and which can tolerate intermittent connectivity. A final question to consider: which of your services must remain on-premises, and how will you measure acceptable latency when they communicate with cloud services?

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Hybrid Cloud
Hybrid cloud networking explained

A unified network that spans private data centers and public cloud, allowing controlled sharing of data and services with secure connectivity and managed routing.

Driver: Compliance & data residency — keep sensitive data in place while leveraging cloud services.
Driver: Migration path — move workloads gradually without disruption.
Driver: Disaster recovery & burst capacity — use cloud capacity when needed.
Enterprise example
Imagine ERP running on-premises for compliance. Analytics run in AWS and access operational data over an encrypted tunnel. Development and test environments run in AWS to leverage elasticity. This split preserves regulatory controls while accelerating innovation.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Hybrid networks let you place workloads where they best meet compliance, performance, and cost goals while keeping them connected.

screens.title: AWS Connectivity Options: VPN vs Direct Connect
screens.narratorSegment: AWS offers multiple hybrid connectivity options and choosing the right one depends on your workload needs. Site-to-Site VPN delivers encrypted tunnels over the public internet, making it quick to deploy and cost-effective for moderate bandwidth requirements or temporary connections. Direct Connect provides a private, dedicated connection with predictable bandwidth and lower latency, but it typically requires longer provisioning and a higher cost. Transit Gateway with VPN or Direct Connect attachments enables central routing for many VPCs and multiple on-premises sites. A practical approach is to use Site-to-Site VPN when you need a rapid, encrypted connection, or as a backup to Direct Connect to maintain high availability. A common misconception is to assume VPN cannot be reliable; while internet variability affects performance, careful routing and using dual tunnels for redundancy substantially mitigates risk. When you estimate traffic, consider whether peak loads can fit over a VPN link and whether the business can tolerate occasional latency spikes. In short: use VPN for speed and flexibility, Direct Connect for predictable, sustained high throughput, and Transit Gateway to centralize routing at scale. AWS Connectivity Options: VPN vs Direct Connect means use site-to-site vpn for quick, encrypted connections and direct connect for dedicated, consistent performance; consider transit gateway for centralized routing.. In practical terms, trade-offs in bandwidth, latency, cost, and setup time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Connectivity Options
Site-to-Site VPN
  • Encrypted tunnels over the public internet using IPsec and IKE.
  • Quick to deploy and cost-effective for moderate bandwidth.
  • Performance subject to internet variability; ideal for backups and temporary links.
When to choose VPN: moderate bandwidth, fast setup, or backup to Direct Connect.
Direct Connect & Transit Gateway
  • Direct Connect: private dedicated links with predictable throughput and lower latency.
  • Transit Gateway: centralizes routing across multiple VPCs and on-premises attachments.
  • Typically higher setup time and cost but better performance for production workloads.
When to choose Direct Connect: sustained high throughput and low latency needs.
Comparison at a glance
Bandwidth: VPN — moderate; Direct Connect — high
Latency: VPN — variable; Direct Connect — low
Setup time: VPN — quick; Direct Connect — longer

screens.title: AWS Site-to-Site VPN Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: An AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection links a Customer Gateway representing your on-premises device with a Virtual Private Gateway attached to a VPC. AWS automatically provisions two independent IPsec tunnels, each terminating at a different AWS endpoint, so that if one tunnel becomes unavailable traffic can fail over to the other. The VGW acts as the VPN concentrator for the VPC — it accepts incoming VPN connections and integrates with VPC route tables to direct traffic to the appropriate subnets. The CGW is an AWS resource that records your device’s public IP and optional BGP autonomous system number for dynamic routing. Route propagation ensures that the VPC route tables receive routes learned from the VPN and that your on-premises routers learn VPC CIDRs when using BGP. A frequent misunderstanding is thinking that the VGW is a physical appliance; it is a logical construct that AWS manages. For high availability, verify both tunnels are configured and that routes prefer the healthy tunnel. A question to reflect on: how will your routing behave if one tunnel drops and route propagation is delayed? AWS Site-to-Site VPN Architecture means vgw and cgw are the vpn endpoints; two ipsec tunnels provide redundancy and routing determines failover behavior.. In practical terms, vgw, cgw, dual ipsec tunnels, and route propagation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › VPN Architecture
Components
  • Virtual Private Gateway (VGW): logical VPN concentrator attached to a single VPC.
  • Customer Gateway (CGW): AWS representation of your on-premises VPN device, including its public IP and optional BGP ASN.
  • Dual IPsec tunnels: two independent tunnels for redundancy and failover.
Example routing behavior
Key Takeaway

Route propagation and routing preferences determine how traffic fails over between the two tunnels — ensure on-premises routers and VPC route tables are configured to learn and prefer the healthy path.

Visual summary
On-premises CGW (public IP)
↕ IPsec tunnel 1 — ESP + IKE
↕ IPsec tunnel 2 — ESP + IKE (redundant)
VGW attached to VPC — routes propagate to VPC route tables
Remember: VGW is logical and attaches to exactly one VPC. If you need centralized routing between multiple VPCs and on-premises networks, consider Transit Gateway attachments.

screens.title: IPsec, ESP and IKE — How the VPN is Secured
screens.narratorSegment: IPsec is the suite used to secure IP communications for Site-to-Site VPN connections. It operates at Layer 3 and provides three core security guarantees: confidentiality, integrity, and authentication. Within IPsec, ESP — Encapsulating Security Payload — is the primary mechanism used by AWS VPN; it encrypts packet payloads and provides authentication so the data cannot be read or tampered with. Authentication Header is an earlier IPsec component that provides integrity but not encryption; AWS VPN mainly uses ESP for the privacy it provides. Key exchange is handled by IKE, the Internet Key Exchange protocol: IKE negotiates SA parameters and establishes the shared keys used by ESP. When a tunnel forms, the endpoints perform cryptographic negotiation, agree on algorithms and lifetime values, and then begin secure packet transport. A common misconception is that encryption alone solves all security concerns; you also need strong authentication, key management, and attention to routing and firewall rules. To test understanding, ask yourself: what would happen if IKE negotiations used mismatched parameters on each side? IPsec, ESP and IKE — How the VPN is Secured means esp provides encryption and authentication for vpn payloads; ike negotiates keys and parameters that both endpoints must match exactly.. In practical terms, protocol roles: confidentiality, integrity, and key exchange. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › IPsec & IKE
IPsec roles
  • Confidentiality: encryption of payload (ESP).
  • Integrity: verification that packets were not altered.
  • Authentication: confirming the communicating parties.
AWS Site-to-Site VPN primarily uses ESP for encryption and authentication, while IKE negotiates the cryptographic keys and SA parameters used by ESP.
Misconception check
Encryption alone does not guarantee connectivity. If IKE negotiations fail due to mismatched algorithms or lifetimes, tunnels will not establish, even if keys are present. Also confirm NAT handling so UDP 500 and 4500 are not blocked.
Key Takeaway

IKE and ESP work together: IKE negotiates keys and parameters; ESP uses them to encrypt and authenticate traffic.

screens.title: How a VPN Tunnel is Established
screens.narratorSegment: Establishing an IPsec VPN tunnel is a multi-step process that begins with IKE negotiation and ends with secure packet exchange. First, the two endpoints discover each other by IP and begin IKE Phase 1 where they authenticate and agree on a secure channel for key exchange. Second, in IKE Phase 2 they negotiate Security Associations that specify encryption and hashing algorithms, Diffie-Hellman groups for key material, and lifetime settings. After successful negotiation, ESP begins protecting packets using the agreed SAs. AWS provisions two tunnels automatically; each tunnel goes through the same negotiation independently to achieve redundancy. If any parameter differs between your on-premises device and AWS configuration — encryption cipher, hash algorithm, or lifetime — the negotiation will fail and the tunnel will not establish. Also consider NAT: if your device is behind NAT, ensure NAT Traversal is enabled so the endpoints use UDP port 4500 when needed. Finally, routing updates or static routes direct traffic into the tunnel. A useful test is to bring up one tunnel and verify data flow before switching to dynamic routing to validate route propagation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Tunnel Establishment
Step-by-step
1. Peer discovery and IKE Phase 1: authenticate endpoints and create a secure channel for negotiation.
2. IKE Phase 2 (SA negotiation): agree encryption, hashing, Diffie-Hellman group, and lifetime values.
3. ESP transport: begin transporting encrypted and authenticated packets using the negotiated SAs.
4. Routing: propagate or add routes so traffic uses the new secure path.
Because AWS provisions two tunnels, repeat this process for each tunnel endpoint. Validate each tunnel independently and then confirm route failover behavior.
Quick checklist
  • Matching IPsec parameters on both sides
  • Pre-shared key entered correctly
  • UDP 500 and 4500 allowed through firewalls
  • Public IP of CGW is reachable

screens.title: Customer Gateway Configuration Parameters
screens.narratorSegment: When configuring your on-premises Customer Gateway device, you must precisely match the parameters AWS expects for the VPN connection. Typical parameters include the pre-shared key for authentication, an agreed encryption algorithm for confidentiality, a hashing algorithm for integrity, a Diffie-Hellman group for key exchange strength, and SA lifetimes that both endpoints honor. Mismatched parameters are a frequent cause of tunnel negotiation failures. For NAT'd devices, enable NAT Traversal and ensure UDP ports 500 and 4500 are open. Also provide your public-facing IP in the CGW resource in AWS to allow AWS tunnels to reach your device. A practical way to reduce errors is to use the AWS-provided VPN configuration snippets for your vendor and copy parameters exactly into the device. Remember: changing lifetime or crypto algorithms on one side without updating the other will drop the tunnel, so document your chosen settings. When you test, bring up tunnels and observe IKE logs to confirm successful negotiation and SA establishment. Customer Gateway Configuration Parameters means match ipsec parameters exactly on both sides, open udp 500/4500, and ensure the cgw public ip is reachable to establish tunnels.. In practical terms, common ipsec settings and avoiding mismatches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › CGW Parameters
Common parameters
  • Pre-shared key (PSK) — must match AWS configuration.
  • Encryption algorithm — provides confidentiality.
  • Hashing algorithm — ensures integrity.
  • Diffie-Hellman group — dictates key exchange strength.
  • SA lifetime — must be coordinated on both sides.
NAT & firewall notes

screens.title: Static Routing vs. Dynamic Routing (BGP)
screens.narratorSegment: Routing is a central design decision when connecting on-premises networks to AWS. You can use static routes in the VPN configuration when the set of remote networks is small and unlikely to change. Static routing is simple but requires manual updates for new prefixes. Dynamic routing with BGP allows automatic exchange of route information between your on-premises router and AWS when you supply a BGP autonomous system number for the Customer Gateway. BGP supports scalable networks and can adapt quickly to failover events, because route changes propagate automatically. However, BGP adds operational complexity and requires correct ASN and prefix filtering to avoid route leaks. A common error is forgetting to advertise on-premises prefixes or incorrectly filtering BGP advertisements, which results in reachability holes despite tunnels being up. screens.title: Troubleshooting & Common Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Tunnel establishment failures and traffic black-holing are commonly caused by a small set of predictable mistakes. First, mismatched IPsec parameters or an incorrect pre-shared key prevent IKE negotiation. Second, using an incorrect public IP in the Customer Gateway record — for example, entering an internal NAT address instead of the external address — means AWS cannot reach your device. Third, firewalls or NAT devices blocking UDP 500 (IKE) and UDP 4500 (NAT Traversal) will stop negotiations. Fourth, routing misconfiguration means that even when tunnels are up, traffic may not be forwarded into them; check VPC route tables and on-premises router entries. To troubleshoot, inspect IKE logs for negotiation errors, confirm the external IP and port reachability using basic network tests, and validate that both sides have matching crypto settings. A practical tip is to bring up one tunnel and test reachability before enabling route propagation or dynamic routing. Finally, document your configuration so that updates to crypto or lifetimes are applied to both sides simultaneously. Ask: which check will you run first when a newly created tunnel remains DOWN? screens.title: High Availability and Failover Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: High availability for hybrid connectivity is achieved through redundancy and thoughtful routing. AWS provides two independent IPsec tunnels; ensure both are configured on your device so that loss of one tunnel routes traffic to the other. For production-critical links, use Direct Connect for primary traffic and configure Site-to-Site VPN as an active or standby backup. During failover, route preferences and route propagation behavior determine how quickly traffic switches paths. With BGP you gain faster automatic failover because routes are withdrawn or re-advertised; with static routing you must ensure that routing policies explicitly direct traffic to the alternate tunnel when needed. Test failover regularly: simulate a tunnel outage and confirm on-premises traffic reaches the cloud via the secondary path and that route tables update or maintain correct preferences. A typical mistake is to assume that both tunnels are automatically equal; routing and BGP attributes will determine which path is preferred. Reflect: how will you validate failover in a way that won’t disrupt production workloads? High Availability and Failover Patterns means use dual tunnels and routing controls; for critical workloads pair direct connect with vpn as a backup and test failover behavior regularly.. fullNarratorScript:
Hybrid cloud networking is the practice of linking an organization’s private data center with public cloud services so data and applications can move between both environments securely and reliably. You will learn why enterprises choose hybrid models — for compliance, data residency, staggered migration, disaster recovery, and predictable burst capacity — and how networking is the backbone that makes those benefits real. This chapter focuses on AWS Site-to-Site VPN: a practical, internet-based, encrypted connection that can be deployed quickly and used as a primary or backup link. We will look at the core components you must provision in AWS and on-premises, explain the role of IPsec, IKE, and ESP in establishing secure tunnels, and point out the common configuration mistakes that cause tunnel failures. By the end you will be able to decide when Site-to-Site VPN is the right choice, identify VGW and CGW roles, and enumerate a concise checklist for a reliable deployment. Think about a real system you manage: what on-premises service would you move behind a VPN first, and why?

These learning objectives map to the practical skills you need to design and operate hybrid connectivity with AWS. First, you will explain hybrid cloud networking: what it is, why enterprises use it, and the scenarios where hybrid models win. Second, you will identify all the components of an AWS Site-to-Site VPN — Virtual Private Gateway, Customer Gateway, and the dual IPsec tunnels — and describe each component’s role in establishing secure connectivity. Third, you will differentiate between hybrid connectivity options such as Site-to-Site VPN and Direct Connect, deciding where each is appropriate based on bandwidth, latency, and cost. Fourth, you will describe how IPsec and IKE secure communications and recognize common design patterns and pitfalls when integrating on-premises networks with AWS. Each objective links a conceptual understanding to practical activities you will perform: planning, provisioning, and troubleshooting a VPN-based connection. Keep these objectives in mind as questions you can answer with a checklist or configuration plan.

Beyond conceptual knowledge, these objectives emphasize practical checks you will perform during a hybrid deployment. You will learn to verify the public IP and NAT posture of your on-premises gateway so AWS can reach its peer. You will learn to match IPsec parameters and pre-shared keys precisely to avoid tunnel negotiation failures. You will learn to check route propagation and ensure that VPC route tables and on-premises routers both know how to reach each other’s CIDRs. Finally, you will acquire the ability to choose a connectivity option: for moderate bandwidth and quick setup, Site-to-Site VPN often fits; for dedicated, low-latency needs, Direct Connect may be preferred. Each of these objectives links to a hands-on validation step you can test in your environment. After this chapter, you should be able to produce a short deployment checklist and a troubleshooting flow for tunnel and routing problems.

Hybrid cloud networking connects an organization’s on-premises systems with public cloud infrastructure so applications and data can operate across both environments securely. The defining trait is seamless, managed connectivity that preserves trust boundaries for sensitive workloads while enabling elasticity for others. Major drivers include compliance and data residency rules that require certain datasets to remain on-premises, phased migration strategies where legacy systems stay local while new services run in the cloud, disaster recovery plans that use the cloud as a secondary site, and burst capacity needs for seasonal peaks. For example, a company may keep its ERP on-premises for regulatory reasons but use AWS for analytics and development: analytics jobs access operational data across a VPN and run on scalable cloud instances. A common misconception is assuming hybrid equals slow; properly designed links, route planning, and placement of latency-sensitive services avoid performance bottlenecks. To design responsibly, inventory which applications need low latency, which require encryption in transit, and which can tolerate intermittent connectivity. A final question to consider: which of your services must remain on-premises, and how will you measure acceptable latency when they communicate with cloud services?

AWS offers multiple hybrid connectivity options and choosing the right one depends on your workload needs. Site-to-Site VPN delivers encrypted tunnels over the public internet, making it quick to deploy and cost-effective for moderate bandwidth requirements or temporary connections. Direct Connect provides a private, dedicated connection with predictable bandwidth and lower latency, but it typically requires longer provisioning and a higher cost. Transit Gateway with VPN or Direct Connect attachments enables central routing for many VPCs and multiple on-premises sites. A practical approach is to use Site-to-Site VPN when you need a rapid, encrypted connection, or as a backup to Direct Connect to maintain high availability. A common misconception is to assume VPN cannot be reliable; while internet variability affects performance, careful routing and using dual tunnels for redundancy substantially mitigates risk. When you estimate traffic, consider whether peak loads can fit over a VPN link and whether the business can tolerate occasional latency spikes. In short: use VPN for speed and flexibility, Direct Connect for predictable, sustained high throughput, and Transit Gateway to centralize routing at scale. AWS Connectivity Options: VPN vs Direct Connect means use site-to-site vpn for quick, encrypted connections and direct connect for dedicated, consistent performance; consider transit gateway for centralized routing.. In practical terms, trade-offs in bandwidth, latency, cost, and setup time. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection links a Customer Gateway representing your on-premises device with a Virtual Private Gateway attached to a VPC. AWS automatically provisions two independent IPsec tunnels, each terminating at a different AWS endpoint, so that if one tunnel becomes unavailable traffic can fail over to the other. The VGW acts as the VPN concentrator for the VPC — it accepts incoming VPN connections and integrates with VPC route tables to direct traffic to the appropriate subnets. The CGW is an AWS resource that records your device’s public IP and optional BGP autonomous system number for dynamic routing. Route propagation ensures that the VPC route tables receive routes learned from the VPN and that your on-premises routers learn VPC CIDRs when using BGP. A frequent misunderstanding is thinking that the VGW is a physical appliance; it is a logical construct that AWS manages. For high availability, verify both tunnels are configured and that routes prefer the healthy tunnel. A question to reflect on: how will your routing behave if one tunnel drops and route propagation is delayed? AWS Site-to-Site VPN Architecture means vgw and cgw are the vpn endpoints; two ipsec tunnels provide redundancy and routing determines failover behavior.. In practical terms, vgw, cgw, dual ipsec tunnels, and route propagation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

IPsec is the suite used to secure IP communications for Site-to-Site VPN connections. It operates at Layer 3 and provides three core security guarantees: confidentiality, integrity, and authentication. Within IPsec, ESP — Encapsulating Security Payload — is the primary mechanism used by AWS VPN; it encrypts packet payloads and provides authentication so the data cannot be read or tampered with. Authentication Header is an earlier IPsec component that provides integrity but not encryption; AWS VPN mainly uses ESP for the privacy it provides. Key exchange is handled by IKE, the Internet Key Exchange protocol: IKE negotiates SA parameters and establishes the shared keys used by ESP. When a tunnel forms, the endpoints perform cryptographic negotiation, agree on algorithms and lifetime values, and then begin secure packet transport. A common misconception is that encryption alone solves all security concerns; you also need strong authentication, key management, and attention to routing and firewall rules. To test understanding, ask yourself: what would happen if IKE negotiations used mismatched parameters on each side? IPsec, ESP and IKE — How the VPN is Secured means esp provides encryption and authentication for vpn payloads; ike negotiates keys and parameters that both endpoints must match exactly.. In practical terms, protocol roles: confidentiality, integrity, and key exchange. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Establishing an IPsec VPN tunnel is a multi-step process that begins with IKE negotiation and ends with secure packet exchange. First, the two endpoints discover each other by IP and begin IKE Phase 1 where they authenticate and agree on a secure channel for key exchange. Second, in IKE Phase 2 they negotiate Security Associations that specify encryption and hashing algorithms, Diffie-Hellman groups for key material, and lifetime settings. After successful negotiation, ESP begins protecting packets using the agreed SAs. AWS provisions two tunnels automatically; each tunnel goes through the same negotiation independently to achieve redundancy. If any parameter differs between your on-premises device and AWS configuration — encryption cipher, hash algorithm, or lifetime — the negotiation will fail and the tunnel will not establish. Also consider NAT: if your device is behind NAT, ensure NAT Traversal is enabled so the endpoints use UDP port 4500 when needed. Finally, routing updates or static routes direct traffic into the tunnel. A useful test is to bring up one tunnel and verify data flow before switching to dynamic routing to validate route propagation.

When configuring your on-premises Customer Gateway device, you must precisely match the parameters AWS expects for the VPN connection. Typical parameters include the pre-shared key for authentication, an agreed encryption algorithm for confidentiality, a hashing algorithm for integrity, a Diffie-Hellman group for key exchange strength, and SA lifetimes that both endpoints honor. Mismatched parameters are a frequent cause of tunnel negotiation failures. For NAT'd devices, enable NAT Traversal and ensure UDP ports 500 and 4500 are open. Also provide your public-facing IP in the CGW resource in AWS to allow AWS tunnels to reach your device. A practical way to reduce errors is to use the AWS-provided VPN configuration snippets for your vendor and copy parameters exactly into the device. Remember: changing lifetime or crypto algorithms on one side without updating the other will drop the tunnel, so document your chosen settings. When you test, bring up tunnels and observe IKE logs to confirm successful negotiation and SA establishment. Customer Gateway Configuration Parameters means match ipsec parameters exactly on both sides, open udp 500/4500, and ensure the cgw public ip is reachable to establish tunnels.. In practical terms, common ipsec settings and avoiding mismatches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Routing is a central design decision when connecting on-premises networks to AWS. You can use static routes in the VPN configuration when the set of remote networks is small and unlikely to change. Static routing is simple but requires manual updates for new prefixes. Dynamic routing with BGP allows automatic exchange of route information between your on-premises router and AWS when you supply a BGP autonomous system number for the Customer Gateway. BGP supports scalable networks and can adapt quickly to failover events, because route changes propagate automatically. However, BGP adds operational complexity and requires correct ASN and prefix filtering to avoid route leaks. A common error is forgetting to advertise on-premises prefixes or incorrectly filtering BGP advertisements, which results in reachability holes despite tunnels being up. Use static routing for small, stable networks and BGP when you need scalable dynamic reachability or when you expect route changes. Think about whether you want route automation during failover or prefer explicit control via static entries. Tunnel establishment failures and traffic black-holing are commonly caused by a small set of predictable mistakes. First, mismatched IPsec parameters or an incorrect pre-shared key prevent IKE negotiation. Second, using an incorrect public IP in the Customer Gateway record — for example, entering an internal NAT address instead of the external address — means AWS cannot reach your device. Third, firewalls or NAT devices blocking UDP 500 (IKE) and UDP 4500 (NAT Traversal) will stop negotiations. Fourth, routing misconfiguration means that even when tunnels are up, traffic may not be forwarded into them; check VPC route tables and on-premises router entries. To troubleshoot, inspect IKE logs for negotiation errors, confirm the external IP and port reachability using basic network tests, and validate that both sides have matching crypto settings. A practical tip is to bring up one tunnel and test reachability before enabling route propagation or dynamic routing. High availability for hybrid connectivity is achieved through redundancy and thoughtful routing. AWS provides two independent IPsec tunnels; ensure both are configured on your device so that loss of one tunnel routes traffic to the other. For production-critical links, use Direct Connect for primary traffic and configure Site-to-Site VPN as an active or standby backup. During failover, route preferences and route propagation behavior determine how quickly traffic switches paths. With BGP you gain faster automatic failover because routes are withdrawn or re-advertised; with static routing you must ensure that routing policies explicitly direct traffic to the alternate tunnel when needed. Test failover regularly: simulate a tunnel outage and confirm on-premises traffic reaches the cloud via the secondary path and that route tables update or maintain correct preferences.
